parts.note: the nursery rhyme 'Ride a cock-horse' sends its rider to a market-town landmark in Oxfordshire, so the ride is set to a song

explanation.surface: A tourist asks where a famous Oxfordshire horse ride set to music took place.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'musical ride' is the nursery rhyme 'Ride a cock-horse to Banbury Cross', a sung rhyme; Banbury is a market town in Oxfordshire and its Cross is the monument the rider heads for.
explanation.definitionFit: The rhyme's destination is that monument in the Oxfordshire town, the scene of its famous ride.

clue.text: External combustion at the end of the primrose way

definitions.text: External combustion at the end of the primrose way

parts.words: External combustion at the end of the primrose way
parts.note: Macbeth's porter speaks of those who go 'the primrose way to the everlasting' fire, an outdoor blaze at the path's end

explanation.surface: A mock-engineering phrase about burning things outdoors at the end of a garden path.
explanation.walkthrough: In 'Macbeth' the porter talks of those 'that go the primrose way to the everlasting bonfire'; 'External combustion' plays on 'internal combustion' for a fire outdoors.
explanation.definitionFit: An open-air fire is combustion outside, and Shakespeare puts an everlasting one at the end of the primrose path.

clue.text: One makes a million with them

definitions.text: One makes a million with them

parts.words: One makes a million with them
parts.note: read 'One' as the digit 1: followed by six zeros it is the figure for a million

explanation.surface: A tip on how a person gets rich.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One makes a million' sounds like someone getting rich, but it is the digit 1, which becomes a million when followed by six zeros.
explanation.definitionFit: Zeros are the symbols written after the digit 1 to form the figure 1,000,000.

indicators.note: badly suggests the letters of the two words are poorly arranged and must be put right

explanation.surface: Someone who has turned out poorly because they had no schooling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Badly' signals the anagram of TURNED OUT.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone untaught has had no tuition or schooling.

parts.note: a unit of three feet, so six feet is a pair of them

explanation.surface: A measurement query about six feet.
explanation.walkthrough: A yard is three feet, so six feet is two yards.
explanation.definitionFit: Six feet of length equals a pair of the three-foot units of imperial measure.

parts.note: a soldier of the line in the 'thin red line', the British infantry at Balaclava

explanation.surface: A skinny football assistant referee.
explanation.walkthrough: 'linesman' suggests a match official, but it is a soldier of the line: the 'thin red line' was the British infantry at Balaclava, whose uniform was red coats.
explanation.definitionFit: A British soldier of former times wore a red uniform jacket, and such troops formed the 'thin red line'.

parts.note: read literally: a product that cleans your scalp and hair, rather than something soaring above you

explanation.surface: A remark that something went clean over the listeners' heads.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clean over your heads' sounds like something not understood, but it means washing the tops of your heads.
explanation.definitionFit: Hair wash is the product used to clean the top of the head.

parts.note: say 'archaic' and its start sounds like 'ark', so 'pre-archaic' suggests before Noah's ark and the Flood

explanation.surface: Someone considers whether calling a thing older than archaic is a good idea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sound idea' seems to mean 'good idea', but it tells you to listen: 'pre-archaic' sounds like 'pre-ark', before Noah's Flood, which the answer literally means.
explanation.definitionFit: Literally 'before the Deluge', the word describes something absurdly old, older than Noah's ark.

parts.note: read 'action' as a lawsuit: a court that throws a claimant's case out before judgment does this to them

explanation.surface: Something or someone has been disabled and can no longer work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put out of action' suggests disabling a machine or a player, but 'action' is the legal word for a lawsuit, and the answer is the judge's ruling that ends one.
explanation.definitionFit: In law, to stop a plaintiff's suit for want of a case is to dismiss their action.

parts.note: the unit is defined by the angle at a circle's centre that cuts off an arc as long as the radius

explanation.surface: A geometry lesson about particular angles found at the middle of a figure.
explanation.definitionFit: This angular unit is defined as the angle subtended at a circle's centre by an arc equal to its radius.

clue.text: What's the hosier needin' in his business ?

definitions.text: What's the hosier needin' in his business ?

parts.words: What's the hosier needin' in his business ?
parts.note: a seller of hosiery deals in stockings; dropping the g, as 'needin'' does

explanation.surface: A dialect question about what a sock seller needs for his shop.
explanation.walkthrough: The dropped g of 'needin'' tells you to drop it from the hosier's goods too: a hosier's trade is in stockings, so 'stockin' trade'.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means the basic goods or resources a business relies on.

indicators.note: to describe a figure is to draw round it, as a compass describes a circle, so one set of letters goes around the other

parts.note: with its negative IN taken away, inept leaves EPT, the jocular back-formation meaning apt; the question mark flags the liberty
IT is a pronoun
HE is a second pronoun

explanation.surface: A grammar teacher criticises an adjective for describing pronouns badly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'describing' looks like part of the definition, but it means drawing a line around something, the way a compass describes a circle. The question mark admits that 'inept' is being cut down to its jocular opposite.
explanation.definitionFit: A descriptive word or phrase attached to a name is an adjective in the broad sense grammarians use.

parts.note: the Archer is Sagittarius, and the zodiac sign just before it is the venomous ...

explanation.surface: Someone asks what venomous figure came before a bowman.
explanation.walkthrough: The Archer is the zodiac sign Sagittarius; the sign that comes before it is the Scorpion, whose sting is venomous.
explanation.definitionFit: In the zodiac's order the Scorpion's sign immediately precedes Sagittarius, and scorpions carry venom.

indicators.note: crazy means wild or deranged, so the name's letters are thrown into a new order

parts.note: Sadie Thompson is the heroine of Somerset Maugham's story 'Rain'

explanation.surface: A Miss Thompson has some mad ideas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'crazy' signals the anagram: SADIE rearranged. Miss Sadie Thompson is the South Seas heroine of Maugham's short story 'Rain', later a play and films.
explanation.definitionFit: Notions are thoughts or conceptions, the plain meaning of the plural here.

clue.text: The boxer's or the Neverland pirate's weapon

explanation.surface: A comparison of the weapons of a prizefighter and the pirate captain of Neverland.
explanation.walkthrough: A boxer's punch with the right fist; Captain Hook of 'Peter Pan' has an iron hook in place of his right hand.
explanation.definitionFit: A boxer throws a punch with the right fist, while Peter Pan's captain wears an iron hook on his right arm.

parts.note: a hot-headed person, read literally, has a fiery red head of hair, called ginger
pop is an informal word for father

explanation.surface: A soothing drink for a short-tempered father.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hot-headed' seems to mean short-tempered, but here it is red-haired: ginger in British slang. POP is father.
explanation.definitionFit: A fizzy ginger-flavoured soft drink is a refreshment.

parts.note: the missing word completes the first line of Wordsworth's Lucy poem about a girl living by the springs of Dove

explanation.surface: Fill in the gap in a line from a Wordsworth poem.
explanation.walkthrough: The opening line of Wordsworth's poem is 'She dwelt among the untrodden ways', one of his Lucy poems.
explanation.definitionFit: Wordsworth's line describes paths few people walk, so the missing adjective means unvisited.

clue.text: Very soft-hearted roof-worker who owns Glasgow ?

indicators.note: soft-hearted is read as having softness at its heart, so the musical marking goes into the middle of the worker

parts.note: a tiler lays tiles on roofs
pp, pianissimo, is the musical marking for very soft

explanation.surface: A kindly roofer who apparently owns the city of Glasgow.
explanation.walkthrough: The music-hall song 'I Belong to Glasgow' says that after a few drinks on a Saturday 'Glasgow belongs to me', so the person who owns Glasgow is a drinker. 'soft-hearted' means softness at the centre.
explanation.definitionFit: The song's singer, a habitual drinker, feels he owns Glasgow once he has had a couple of drinks.

clue.text: The famous admiral declaims his piece

indicators.note: spoken in a Cockney accent the admiral's first name loses its opening aitch, so declaiming drops that letter

parts.note: the famous admiral is Horatio Nelson
N is Nelson's initial

explanation.surface: Admiral Nelson stands and recites a speech.
explanation.walkthrough: 'declaims' tells you the admiral's name is spoken aloud with the aitch dropped, as a Cockney would: 'ORATIO N(ELSON).
explanation.definitionFit: A piece declaimed is a formal speech, delivered before an audience.

clue.text: French sculptor who finishes off a Russian composer

indicators.note: the sculptor's name forms the finish of the composer's, so the composer's opening letters are dropped

parts.note: Alexander Borodin was the Russian composer of 'Prince Igor'

explanation.surface: A French artist is accused of killing off a Russian musician.
explanation.walkthrough: 'finishes off' sounds like murder but means 'is the ending of': BORODIN without its first two letters BO.
explanation.definitionFit: Auguste Rodin was the French maker of 'The Thinker' and 'The Kiss'.

indicators.note: outside here means without, so the letters for the City are left out

parts.note: EC is the postal district of the City of London, its financial centre

explanation.surface: An urge to recover a lost thrill outside London's financial district.
explanation.walkthrough: 'outside' looks like a container indicator, but here it means 'without'. The City is London's financial district, known by its postcode. 'Recapture it' makes the whole clue describe a feeling people long to get back.
explanation.definitionFit: Ecstasy is the feeling people long to recapture, and the whole clue describes it.

clue.text: Curious blade found outside the ancient city was made to last

indicators.note: the rearranged letters are found around the city, enclosing it
curious means odd, so the letters of the word are put into a strange order

parts.note: Ur was an ancient city of Mesopotamia, birthplace of Abraham

explanation.surface: An odd knife found beyond the walls of an old city has stood the test of time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Curious' rearranges the knife's letters into DABLE, and 'found outside' puts that round the ancient city of Abraham's birth.
explanation.definitionFit: Something long-lasting is built to endure and resist wear.

parts.note: read as gardening: a seedling is set into a flower bed rather than a child being tucked in

explanation.surface: A parent tucks a child in for the night.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put to bed' suggests sleep, but the bed is a flower bed and the act is setting a plant in the soil.
explanation.definitionFit: To set a plant in a garden bed is to fix it firmly in the ground.

parts.note: the Italian composer of the famous song 'Goodbye', a farewell set to music

explanation.surface: A music teacher making a farewell speech.
explanation.walkthrough: Sir Paolo Tosti wrote the popular Victorian ballad 'Goodbye!', so he is the music-master of farewells; he was also singing master to the British royal family.
explanation.definitionFit: Paolo Tosti, singing teacher to Queen Victoria's family, composed the farewell song 'Goodbye!'.

parts.note: Hamlet tells Claudius that the worm, feeding on corpses, is the supreme ruler where eating is concerned

explanation.surface: Fill in the gap in Hamlet's line about worms.
explanation.walkthrough: Hamlet, Act 4 Scene 3: 'Your worm is your only emperor for diet', mocking Claudius with the thought that kings end as food for worms.
explanation.definitionFit: Hamlet calls the worm the supreme monarch of diet, since every body ends as its meal.

parts.note: read 'flighty' literally: birds that fly but carry a girl's pet name, the sailors' name for the giant petrel

explanation.surface: A disapproving remark about some frivolous young women.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flighty' suggests frivolous, but these girls fly: sailors call the giant petrel a nelly, and Nellie is also a girl's name.
explanation.definitionFit: The giant petrel is known to seamen as a nelly, while Nellie is a pet form of Helen or Eleanor.

clue.text: Sounded as if Victoria slept here

explanation.surface: A guidebook notes a resonant spot where Queen Victoria supposedly stayed the night.
explanation.walkthrough: A Victoria is a variety of plum, so a bed for one is a plum bed; 'Sounded' is measuring depth with a weighted line.
explanation.definitionFit: Measuring water depth with a lead weight on a line; split, the word is a bed for a Victoria, a well-known plum variety.

clue.text: The first picture of the book

definitions.text: The first picture of the book

parts.words: The first picture of the book
parts.note: the illustration facing the title page, the first one a reader meets

explanation.surface: Someone describes the opening illustration in a volume.
explanation.definitionFit: An illustration placed facing a volume's title page is the opening image a reader sees.
